Over the five years to November 2026, two chipmakers in the same industry produced vastly different market returns. The stock of Texas Instruments (TXN) climbed 89.2%, while NXP Semiconductors (NXPI), which makes chips for cars, factories and data centers, rose 34.5%. Was the gap down to faster sales growth, bigger profits, or investors paying more for each dollar of profit?

NXP has done better than most of its industry. Over the five years to November 2026, its stock beat 63.0% of the chipmakers it was compared with. But three companies whose average sales growth over the last three years was within 4 percentage points of NXP’s beat it, Amkor Technology (AMKR) among them. Each beat NXP by at least 20 points over five years, and the table shows the other two. Texas Instruments came out 54.6 points ahead.
Total return to 2026-11-12, including dividends. Companies in Semiconductors whose sales grew within 4 points of NXPI’s. P/E: latest close over the last four quarters’ earnings per share.

Analog Devices (ADI) finished further ahead still, beating NXP by 106.3 points. While NXP secured a solid gain for a chipmaker, these three peers performed far better. Analog Devices also more than doubled its sales over that period, up 113.4% against 31.0% for NXP.

Over the last three years, Texas Instruments expanded sales by an average of 5.6% a year, compared with 2.0% for NXP. Over the full five years, though, that order flips. Between 2021 and 2026, NXP’s sales rose 31.0%, while Texas Instruments’ sales rose 18.1%. Faster sales growth cannot explain a five-year gap when NXP’s sales grew more.
Texas Instruments sells chips through two segments, Analog and Embedded Processing: power products that manage how devices use electricity, and microcontrollers that run electronic equipment.

items.t: Will Texas Instruments' 2027 Pricing Strategy Lift Profitability?
sum: Texas Instruments Incorporated TXN is entering its 2027 customer pricing discussions with an opportunity to improve profitability. During its third-quarter 2026 earnings call, management said pricing was flat year over year in the first half of 2026, but some increases emerged in the second half, mainly in Analog.

Texas Instruments typically discusses prices annually. For 2027, it is considering customer demand and the value of securing reliable supply. Tight capacity, particularly outside China and Taiwan, may strengthen TXN’s position. Customers seeking guaranteed supply may accept higher prices, giving the company room to improve revenue per chip.

Texas Instruments’ third-quarter 2026 results show why pricing matters. Third-quarter revenues climbed 28% year over year to $6.06 billion, while gross profit increased 43% to $3.887 billion. Gross margin reached 64.2% compared with 57.4% a year earlier. The company attributed the improvement mainly to increased revenues, higher pricing, improved factory utilization and a better product mix.

However, pricing gains are not guaranteed. Customers may resist increases if chip supply improves or demand weakens. Higher prices could affect customer relationships and order volumes. TXN must balance pricing with its manufacturing investments and ability to deliver dependable supply.

Texas Instruments has not disclosed the expected size or timing of 2027 price changes. It plans to provide more details with its full-year 2026 results in January next year. Favorable supply conditions and stronger demand could help TXN lift profitability in 2027, but the scale of the benefit will depend on the outcome of customer negotiations and market strength.

Analog Devices, Inc. ADI competes with Texas Instruments in analog chips and signal-processing products. In the third quarter of fiscal 2026, ADI's revenues jumped 40% year over year to $4.02 billion.

Analog Devices’ non-GAAP gross margin expanded 330 basis points year over year to 72.5%. Strong demand and manufacturing flexibility supported its performance. Although ADI has not disclosed a specific 2027 pricing target, its results show how product value and demand can support profitability.

What Could Send Texas Instruments Stock Soaring?
sum: For questions about this article or underlying research, email help@trefis.com.

Texas Instruments (TXN) stock returned 73.3% over the past twelve months, against 9.8% for the S&P 500. One fast-growing group of TI’s customers is now buying far more than it did a year ago. Any further climb in the stock depends partly on whether those customers keep buying and whether TI’s factories make enough to supply them. So which customers are those, and how much more are they buying?

Those buyers are TI’s data center customers. On the October 21, 2026 call, management said TI’s sales into the data center market rose about 95% in fiscal Q3 2026 from a year earlier, and about 20% from the quarter before. By management’s estimate, that market is now about 13% of TI’s revenue.

Management said that demand is still rising and that it sees no slowdown in what customers are investing in data centers. TI now sells about 10,000 different parts into this market, a number management said grows every quarter. So far, data center buyers are still buying more.

Data center sales are still a small slice of Texas Instruments, which sold $20.8 billion over the twelve months to September 30, 2026. Management gives no forecast for these sales, and said it does not give guidance by market. Analog chips made up 79.2% of TI’s sales in fiscal 2025. Data center is a market those chips sell into, not a reported segment.

TI can sell more only if it makes more, and management says the slowest part of adding output is done. The company has built its clean rooms, the buildings that take years to finish, and is quickly ramping a new site in Malaysia. On the factory space it needs, TI looks ready so far.

The share price appears to assume much of that growth already. TI trades at 35.6 times its earnings over the past twelve months, against 21.8 for the S&P 500. Even so, the shares sit 15.7% below their highest close of the past year, reached on June 22, 2026.

Although markets have enjoyed a strong run, with the benchmark S&P 500 up 12.45% year to date, the rate background has turned against income investors. Rate-setters raised rates at its September meeting, leaving the upper bound of the federal funds target at 4.00%. On Kalshi, a quarter-point hike at the December 9, 2026 meeting is priced at 80%, against 22% for a hold. But rising rates tend to rattle dividend stocks, because Treasuries and savings accounts start competing for the same income dollars. The 10-year Treasury yield is now at 4.95%, above the yield on every stock below.

The stocks that hold up typically share three traits: rising payouts, earnings that cover those payouts, and cash flow that funds buybacks too. During the last hiking cycle, from March 16, 2022, to July 26, 2023, all four names here finished higher. Automatic Data Processing (NASDAQ:ADP | ADP Price Prediction) jumped 22.36%, Texas Instruments (NASDAQ:TXN) gained 3.42%, Johnson & Johnson (NYSE:JNJ) rose 2.39%, and Cisco Systems (NASDAQ:CSCO) held flat at 0.04%. Each also raised its dividend during that span and during the 2015 to 2018 cycle. We highlighted income plays ahead of September’s Fed meeting, and the case for dividend growth has only strengthened since.

ADP pays $6.80 annually, a 2.24% yield at $304.02. Its $1.70 quarterly payout takes about 60% of fiscal Q1 2027 adjusted EPS of $2.82. Higher rates directly help: interest on client funds jumped 15% to $329.3 million as average balances grew to $36.9 billion. Management lifted fiscal 2027 adjusted EPS growth guidance to 10% to 12%. sum: For questions about this article or underlying research, email help@trefis.com.

Texas Instruments (TXN) stock returned 93.5% over the year to October 30, 2026, beating the 11.3% for the S&P 500. Investors are now paying 38.7 times its earnings over the last four fiscal quarters. That multiple sits above its average of 33.9 at the past twelve fiscal quarter ends. Whether you held through that run or watched it, how much more could the shares be worth if sales keep growing?

Under the scenario outlined below, Texas Instruments shares would be worth about $475.51 three years after the October 30 close. That compares to $300.84 that day, marking an upside of 58.1%, or 16.5% a year with dividends left out. The model assumes revenue grows 17.2% a year, set at 0.85 times its growth over the twelve months to fiscal Q3 2026. It sets the net margin at 70% of today’s figure plus 30% of its average at the twelve quarter ends before the latest one. The P/E stays at today’s level as an assumption rather than a forecast. This holds the multiple at 38.7 three years on, keeping it above the 33.9 average.

Higher sales supply all of the gain and a little more. A slightly lower net margin takes a little back, and the P/E adds nothing. By market, industrial sales rose more than 40%, and data center sales nearly doubled.

Management sees no slowdown, describing growing demand from industrial, automotive and data center customers. Revenue in fiscal Q3 2026 rose 27.7% from a year earlier, faster than the scenario’s pace. Part of that is a recovery. Management said industrial sales only now got back to their fiscal Q3 2022 level, four years later.

Texas Instruments is adding supply to keep up. Management said it can grow capacity every quarter, helped by a new site in Malaysia, and expects capital spending of $2 billion to $3 billion in 2026. Texas Instruments (TXN) has climbed about 60% in 2026, and for most of that run, the story was a simple demand rebound. On August 4, the company gave investors something more specific to hold onto. GE Appliances said it will source roughly one-third of the chips for its new Louisville laundry plant from Texas Instruments starting in 2027, a commitment that nearly doubles GE Appliances’ spending with the company.

GE chose Texas Instruments in part because it runs high-volume semiconductor fabs on U.S. soil, at a moment when supply chain security has become a boardroom priority. That is the advantage the market has been slow to price, and it is worth understanding before deciding whether a stock near $280 still has room to run.
Why a Washing Machine Contract Says Something About the Whole Company

The GE Appliances agreement is small next to Texas Instruments’ $19 billion in trailing revenue. Its value is what it confirms. GE runs a “Zero Distance” strategy built on shortening its supply chain, and it tied the decision to Texas Instruments’ domestic footprint, with chips coming from fabs in Sherman and Richardson, Texas, and Lehi, Utah. That is the same argument management made on the second-quarter earnings call, only from the customer’s side of the table. CEO Haviv Ilan described a market where TI’s inventory and capacity let it win business rivals cannot serve fast enough. “We are seeing examples, real-time examples of, hey, we are line down, please help us. And every time that happens, that’s an opportunity,” Ilan said. When a customer runs out of parts, the supplier that can ship becomes the supplier that keeps the design. A GE-sized commitment, negotiated years ahead of production, is the planned version of that same dynamic.

Texas Instruments plans to invest more than $60 billion across seven fabs in Texas and Utah, and the clean room space it built during the last downcycle now stands ready to absorb demand. That’s changing. TI’s chips sit inside every AI server, regulating and distributing the enormous amounts of power modern GPUs consume. The market has taken notice, rewarding the stock with a forward earnings multiple of roughly 39x, rich for a company historically viewed as a slow-growth cyclical.

TI’s largest end market, industrial, is still recovering. Industrial revenue grew more than 30% year over year last quarter, marking eight straight quarters of sequential growth, yet the segment remains roughly 15% below its prior peak. That gap matters. A recovering cycle with room left to run supports a higher multiple than a business already at the top of its cycle. Earnings should continue to improve as the recovery unfolds. Management guided second-quarter revenue to $5.0 billion to $5.4 billion, well above analyst estimates, with growth expected across both industrial and data center markets.

Every AI server needs more than just GPUs, memory, and networking. It also requires a network of analog chips that convert, regulate, and monitor electricity, synchronize high-speed data flowing between processors and memory, and ensure the system operates reliably under heavy workloads. Without these components, the GPUs cannot be powered or communicate efficiently. As AI servers become larger and more power-intensive, the amount of analog content per server continues to increase.

TI has built the largest data center business in the analog semiconductor industry, generating approximately $1.5 billion in revenue in calendar 2025, up 64% year over year. Capital expenditures totaled $4.6 billion in 2025 but are expected to decline to $2 billion to $3 billion in 2026 as 300 millimeter capacity expansions near completion, and CFO Rafael Lizardi said the company is “on track to deliver more than $8 per share of free cash flow in 2026.”

Weighing Weebit Nano’s Valuation After The Texas Instruments Deal And New 2026 Revenue Guidance
sum: Weebit Nano (ASX:WBT) has drawn fresh attention after licensing its ReRAM technology to Texas Instruments and issuing minimum revenue guidance of A$10 million for fiscal 2026, marking a clear operational milestone.

After the Texas Instruments announcement and new 2026 revenue guidance, interest has picked up. A 30 day share price return of 18.49% and a 1 year total shareholder return of 57.61% point to building momentum rather than fading enthusiasm.
If this kind of semiconductor story has your attention, it could be a good moment to widen your watchlist with other high growth tech and AI stocks that are getting investor interest.

With a 1 year total shareholder return above 50%, fresh minimum revenue guidance of A$10 million for 2026 and a Texas Instruments licensing deal in hand, is there still a buying opportunity here, or is the market already pricing in future growth?
With Weebit Nano last closing at A$4.87, the current P/B of 11.3x places the shares at a premium level compared with both peers and the wider semiconductor group.

The P/B ratio compares the market value of the equity to its book value, so a higher figure usually reflects strong expectations for future value creation relative to the existing balance sheet. For a company that is still loss making, a rich P/B often signals that investors are focusing on potential commercialisation rather than current profitability.

In this case, Weebit Nano is unprofitable, reports a loss of A$38.38m and does not yet have meaningful revenue at around A$4.41m. It is also forecast to remain unprofitable over the next three years. Set against that backdrop, an 11.3x P/B implies the market is placing a high value on future revenue growth rather than current returns on equity, which are negative.
